## Refused or denied commands

A refused or denied command is a stop. Report it in your result's refusals list and do not retry it in another form: not another path to the program, another tool, another wrapper, or another command with the same effect. The one exception: when the refusing guard's or hook's own refusal message names a route (an exact command or tool to use instead), you may take exactly that route, once, and record it as that entry's route; every other form, and every auto-mode classifier denial, stays a stop. A refused or denied command is one that a permission denial, a hook refusal, a sandbox refusal, or the harness's own safety checks (a shell-command checker or an auto-mode classifier) stopped, or one held for an approval that nobody answers; record those last two kinds with refusedBy permission. A command that ran and failed is not a refusal, and the failure rules cover it. Each refusals entry carries command (the command exactly as you wrote it), refusedBy (permission, hook or sandbox), hook (the hook's name when the refusal gave one, else null), route (the route a hook's or the sandbox's own refusal message named and you took, else null), and next (what you did next). An empty list means you met none.
